options.text: A queue, because the bracket opened last is the one that must be checked first

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why nesting needs the newest opener checked first
questions.learningObjective: explain why a last in first out check catches a mis-nested line that a first in first out check passes
questions.stem: A line of text holds four characters: an opening round bracket, an opening square bracket, a closing round bracket, then a closing square bracket. A reader pairs each closing bracket with the opening bracket still waiting, taking the most recent one. Explain why that rule reports a mismatch on this line, and why taking the oldest waiting bracket instead would report the line as balanced.

answer.exemplar: The two rules disagree because the line is mis-nested, and only one of them is entitled to notice. The opening brackets wait in the order round, then square, and the closing round bracket may only match the square bracket, because the square bracket was opened inside the round one and so must close first. Taking the most recent waiting opener pairs the closing round with the square, sees that they do not belong together, and reports the mismatch at the third character, which is where the text is wrong. Taking the oldest waiting opener pairs the closing round with the round bracket and the closing square with the square bracket, finds a match at every character, and reports nothing. That second answer is not a weaker check but a different one: it tests whether the brackets can be paired up at all while ignoring which bracket encloses which, and a line such as this one can be paired up and still be wrongly nested.

questions.explanation: The guarantee a nesting check needs is that the most recent unmatched opener is the only one a closer may match, and that is what a stack provides, so the state the reader keeps is one list of unmatched openers. A queue keeps the same openers in the wrong order, which turns the check into a test of whether the brackets can be paired up at all. The run confirmed the difference on this exact line: taking the newest reported a mismatch at the closing round bracket against the square bracket, while taking the oldest reported the line balanced, and a correctly nested line passed under both rules.
questions.hint: Ask which opening bracket the closing round bracket is allowed to match, and why.

Every element of the names list is still a name and every element of the scores list is still a score, so each list is internally consistent and both pass whatever check the report applies to them. What has been lost is the one thing that mattered, which is which score belonged to which name, and nothing in either list can reveal that it is gone. The run made the loss concrete: names cy, ada, di, bo with scores 4, 1, 3, 2 sorted on their own print ada with 4 and cy with 1, while the true pairings are ada with 1 and cy with 4, so a report that showed all four rows would have been wrong on every row. One list of records, or one list of pairs, removes the fault by making the two facts travel together: a sort then has to move them both or neither, and there is no longer a separate place for one of them to be left behind.

questions.explanation: A fault that is not represented anywhere cannot be detected, and that is the whole mechanism here. The two lists each hold valid values of the right kind, so a report that prints a name and a number produces well-formed output throughout and no check complains. The run confirmed that the name order ada, bo, cy, di read against the untouched score order pairs every name with a score that is not its own, which is four wrong rows rather than a detectable error. Keeping each name with its score in one record removes the possibility rather than reporting it afterwards.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What order buys a range query and what it demands of arrivals
questions.learningObjective: explain the exchange a sorted structure makes between queries and arrivals
questions.stem: A log of readings is kept in order so that a report can count how many of them fall in a given range, and a new reading arrives every second. Explain what the order buys that report, and what it demands of every arrival.

answer.exemplar: Keeping the readings in order buys the report two things it could not otherwise have. A range becomes the span between two bounds, so the count is the distance between the two places the bounds stop, found by walking inward from each end rather than by reading every reading; and a position in the log becomes a fixed number of steps along, so asking for the reading at position 50,000 costs the same whatever the values are. The demand is on every arrival. A new reading cannot simply be appended, because the order it is supposed to be in is somewhere in the middle, so it has to find its place and make room, and in a plain sorted array making room means shifting the tail: a reading that belongs at position 400 of a 1000-reading array moves the 600 readings above it. That is 600 units of movement once a second, against a report that may be asked a handful of times an hour, so the running cost is set entirely by the arrival rate. The design question is therefore not which structure is faster but which of the two rates dominates, and the run priced the upkeep at 600 moves for an arrival at position 400.

questions.explanation: The exchange is between two rates, and both sides of it are countable. Order turns a range query into two inward walks and a position query into a fixed number of steps; upkeep turns every arrival into a shift of the tail, which the run priced at 600 moves for an arrival at position 400 of a 1000-reading array. Whichever of the two happens more often decides the design, and a structure that keeps its own order rather than shifting a flat array is the usual answer when arrivals dominate, because it pays a smaller constant per arrival and keeps the range query available.
questions.hint: Ask how many moves an arrival costs, and how often the query runs compared with the arrivals.
